title: Vector, Time-Series, and Big Data Structures
summary: Recognize when a specialized store or sketch beats a general-purpose database.
keyPoints: A vector index answers similarity questions; exact-key lookup should stay in a normal store.
HNSW favors low latency and high recall; IVF trades some recall for memory control.
Hybrid search combines keyword precision with vector recall, then reranks the merged list.
Time-series stores win on append-heavy writes, time-range reads, compression, and retention.
Bloom filters, HyperLogLog, count-min sketches, and external sort answer large-data questions with bounded resources.
Add a specialized store only when the access pattern or scale justifies another system to operate.

complexity.note: Too slow at millions of vectors.

commonMistakes: Using a vector index for exact lookups or small data sets where a normal index already works.
Reporting ANN latency without measuring recall on real queries.
Putting high-cardinality values in a time-series tag and creating millions of series.
Using a probabilistic sketch for billing or another exact-count requirement.
interviewNotes: Name the query shape first: similarity, time range, membership, cardinality, frequency, or sort.
State the recall or error bound when you choose an approximate structure.
Translate vector count and dimensions into memory before choosing a shard count.
Keep the source of truth in a normal store and treat the vector index as derived.
For retention, say what stays raw, what is rolled up, and for how long.

checkYourself.question: Why is an HNSW index often memory heavy?
checkYourself.answer: It stores the vectors plus a layered proximity graph. That graph improves recall and latency but adds memory beyond the raw vector size.

checkYourself.question: When is a Bloom filter useful?
checkYourself.answer: It can reject keys that are definitely absent before a disk or network lookup. It has no false negatives, but false positives are possible.

checkYourself.question: Why downsample time-series data?
checkYourself.answer: Raw points are expensive to store and most old queries need a trend, not every sample. Rollups cut storage and read cost while keeping recent detail.
